top.line: Technology sovereignty is the ability to move workloads
top.para: Europe's sovereignty talk centres on frontier models, data centres and GPUs, where the ball is, not where it is going. Sovereignty means being able to replace every dot on a Wardley map, tested with twins in QA for the minimum viable company. Ask whether it can move before whether it is cheap, and rely on open source.

in-short.line: Play where the ball is going: make everything replaceable
in-short.para: Frontier models and GPUs take years and capital and favour incumbents. Sovereignty is the ability to move a workload, even within one cloud. Remove each dot from a Wardley map, aim for an alternative that works for the minimum viable company, run twins in QA, ask possible before cheap, and prefer open source.

ball.line: Europe chases frontier models; the ball is mobility
ball.para: A good padel player reads the ball and is already there; moving after it leaves the glass is hopeless. The frontier model, giant data centre and GPU are where the ball is now, needing capital that benefits incumbents. Models are becoming a commodity, so the ball is heading towards moving workloads, data and agent actions.

move.line: Most organisations cannot move workloads, even within one cloud
move.para: Sovereignty is agility, almost liquidity: moving a workload and still operating. Infrastructure hard-coded, created by clicks and never deployed twice is fragile whatever the contract says. It is an engineering gap, and any supplier disruption that stops a business is critical, national infrastructure or not.

dot.line: Remove each dot and follow the edges up
dot.para: On a Wardley map, ask of every dot you do not control what happens if it disappears. If removing object storage stops the service, that blast radius belongs before the board. The rule covers the whole stack, custom-built included, since a system only one person can deploy is also a single point of failure.

zero.line: The alternative must work, not match today's performance
zero.para: Efforts stall by demanding an equally optimised alternative. The bar is that it works for the minimum viable company: priority customers and services that must never stop. Data alone is an archive without software and schema; each uncontrolled dot needs a twin, and services should degrade rather than stop.

qa.line: Twins in disposable QA prove the business can move
qa.para: A disposable QA environment built from nothing on storage, identity and self-hosted model twins proves each time that the business can run without uncontrolled dots. Problems surface on a Tuesday rather than in an outage, and weekly runs close the gap between level 2 and level 3 without a migration project.

possible.line: Ask whether it can move before asking the cost
possible.para: Asking whether sovereignty is cost effective before asking whether it is possible ends the conversation, since the answer is usually not yet. Record a cost and scale matrix per dot, tested last week. The engineering benefits of reproducible, disposable environments should pay for much of it; focus on dots with no alternative.

open.line: Only open source control survives a change of owner
open.para: A European supplier is one acquisition from not being one, and the reverse also holds. Prosus and Dealroom found Europe creates as many AI startups as the US but converts them at a third of the rate, and 44% of 500 US unicorn founders were foreign-born. Europe lacks a commercial open source model.

central.line: Some twins should be shared infrastructure, like roads
central.para: Not every company can build a twin of every dependency alone. Governments, industry bodies and large supply-chain players should provide some centrally, built once, open and used by everyone, without becoming a new dependency. Judo for small countries and Move the cloud, not the code develop this.

now.line: Models finally make dependency mapping affordable at scale
now.para: Mapping every service, removing each dot and simulating the result was always right and always too expensive. Today's models can do it at scale, better on twins that can actually be switched off. Map it, remove the dot, run the twin in QA and put level-0 dependencies on the register with a name.

limits.line: The map is illustrative and the maturity levels uncalibrated
limits.para: The map shows a typical service, not a measured one, and the maturity levels are an uncalibrated proposal. Prosus and Dealroom report parity in AI startups, and the Stanford study covers unicorns to 2021. Minimum viable company is a resilience term, and twins beyond storage are not built.

sources.line: Sources: a voice memo, startup data and twin docs
sources.para: A voice memo of 12 October 2026 after a sovereignty event, written up by this site's agent. Prosus and Dealroom's State of AI in Europe, 16 March 2026, and Ilya Strebulaev's unicorn founder study via Crunchbase News, with twins.sgit.ai and open-source.sgit.ai.
